claim: The report, arXiv 2610.22471, was submitted 15 Oct 2026 (v1) and revised 19 Oct 2026 (v2). It is a preprint/technical report with no venue listed.
The authors' bottom line: GPT-6-Astra has crossed the threshold of embodied competence but not of practical embodied intelligence.
quote: our results suggest that GPT-6-Astra has largely crossed the threshold of embodied competence, but not yet that of practical embodied intelligence.

claim: The evaluation covers 12 benchmarks spanning tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms and dexterous hands.
quote: We conduct a large-scale evaluation across 12 representative benchmarks spanning tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands.

claim: The headline protocol lets the model learn in context from training-set demonstrations and greatly increases the number of execution steps allowed.
quote: Under a unified protocol that allows in-context learning (ICL) from training-set demonstrations and substantially increases the number of execution steps, GPT-6-Astra achieves unprecedented performance

claim: The extended budget allows ten times as many action steps as each benchmark's standard budget.
quote: The extended budget allows ten times as many action steps as the standard budget.

claim: The model weights stay fixed. ICL means the model studies the demonstrations and writes a frozen 'knowledge package' (notes, motion references, code helpers) that it reuses at test time.
quote: During preparation, GPT-6-Astra may analyze the demonstrations and develop task-specific notes and reusable code. These materials form a knowledge package, which is frozen before evaluation and provided to every test episode of that task. GPT-6-Astra’s model weights remain unchanged.

claim: The paper reports near-saturation on LIBERO and SIMPLE, and 81.9% on RoboDojo and 87.3% on DexJoCo, under the extended budget.
quote: it approaches saturation on the LIBERO series and SIMPLE, while achieving 81.9% on RoboDojo and 87.3% on DexJoCo.

claim: Table 2: on RoboDojo the best published SOTA is 29.6%. GPT-6-Astra+ICL scores 81.9% at up to 10x budget, but only 27.6% at the 1x cutoff of that same run, and 54.2% in a separate 1x run that uses a VLA.
Table 2: on Bench2Dex GPT-6-Astra matches pi0.5 at the standard budget (25.6 vs 25.5) and reaches 61.5% only with the 10x budget.
On SIMPLE, task-level ICL raises standard-budget success from 70.8% (zero-shot) to 90.8%.
quote: task-level ICL raises standard-budget success on the four common tasks from 70.8% to 90.8%

claim: Cost is high: on LIBERO-Long++ each episode takes about a million tokens and nearly an hour, and on LIBERO-Ultra-Long about nine million tokens and nearly two hours.
quote: each episode still consumes about a million tokens and nearly an hour of inference and tool use; on LIBERO-Ultra-Long, these costs rise to roughly nine million tokens and nearly two hours

claim: On RoboDojo, one episode under the extended budget averages more than three hours.
quote: on RoboDojo, a single episode under the extended budget takes more than three hours on average.

claim: The authors estimate cost at roughly 1 USD per 1M tokens, because about 98% of the tokens are cached input.
quote: the vast majority of tokens consumed are cached input tokens (approximately 98% in our runs). Accordingly, we use a simple rule of thumb for cost estimation: 1M tokens  1 USD.

claim: Harness ablation on RoboDojo: standalone VLA 6.91%, open-loop 5.83%, ICL plus closed-loop VLA 54.17% at 19.335M tokens.
quote: Combining ICL with closed-loop VLA achieves the highest success rate of 54.17%, exceeding the best non-ICL closed-loop configuration by 28.34 percentage points, but consumes 19.335 million tokens

claim: Direct joint-angle control does worse than end-effector commands.
quote: directional motion commands improve the average success rate by 2.50 percentage points, whereas direct joint-angle control leads to a 5.84-percentage-point drop.

claim: Real-world, zero-shot on 8 platforms: rigid pick-and-place 17/18, cloth folding 2/4, plug insertion 0/11, navigation and search 9/23.
quote: rigid pick-and-place is reliable (17/18 trials) and matches simulation, whereas deformable objects (e.g., cloth folding: 2/4 on the Franka 3), precise contact (e.g., plug insertion: 0/11 across three platforms) and long-horizon mobile tasks (e.g., navigation and search: 9/23 on the AgileX Tracer) remain markedly harder.

claim: Active vision: on a dual-arm robot, the model moved its free arm so the wrist camera could see the vase mouth, then completed the insertion.
quote: GPT-6-Astra moves the free arm until its wrist camera looks at the vase mouth, and then completes the insertion

claim: On the Unitree G1 humanoid, the model spends about 90% of each run deliberating, and one manipulation trial takes over an hour.
quote: on the G1, GPT-6-Astra spends about 90% of each run deliberating, and a single manipulation trial takes over an hour.

claim: Hand-written context matters: on the Tianji hands, the model completed 0/3 grasps without predefined grasp primitives and 3/3 with human-written ones.
quote: without predefined grasp primitives GPT-6-Astra did not complete a single grasp (0/3), whereas with human-written grasp primitives it succeeded in 3/3.

claim: In the household prototype, where the world clock keeps running, an egg charred because the model took about 8 s of world time to decide to turn the burner off.
quote: deciding takes 8 s of world time with the burner still on, and by the time the burner is turned off, about 90 s after the egg has set, the egg has charred.

claim: In the household prototype, the model left a refrigerator door open from 300 s to 765 s of world time.
quote: the door stays open from 300 s to 765 s of world time.

claim: The authors say benchmark results depend heavily on conditions the benchmarks provide: in-context access to demonstrations and an extended step budget in which failures cost nothing.
quote: GPT-6-Astra’s results on established embodied benchmarks depend heavily on conditions that the benchmarks grant.

claim: Simulators pause while the model thinks. On RoboDojo, standard budgets equal 8–76 s of commanded motion, against an average of 55 minutes of computation.
quote: on RoboDojo, the standard budgets correspond to 8–76 s of commanded motion against an average of 55 minutes of computation

claim: The real-robot runs used gpt-6-astra through the OpenAI Responses API at maximum reasoning effort.
quote: Tool calls through the OpenAI Responses API (gpt-6-astra, reasoning effort max, mode pro, store=false)

claim: The project page's TL;DR: embodied competence, largely yes; practical embodied intelligence, not yet.
quote: Embodied competence — largely yes. Practical embodied intelligence — not yet.

claim: Independent preprint (Zhang et al.): GPT-6 Astra reached 22.48% average success on RoboDojo over 2,100 trials, ranking above every public entry, while GPT-5.5 reached only 0.88%.
quote: GPT-6 Astra achieves 22.48% average success rate and 28.97 Score over 2,100 trials, ranking above every public entry. Yet GPT-5.5 and DeepSeek-Flash reach only 0.88% and 1.92% average success rate

claim: Zhang et al. found no aggregate benefit from one-shot demonstrations. This conflicts with the SenseNova report's ICL gains.
quote: In-context experiments show no aggregate benefit from one-shot demonstrations

claim: Zhang et al. halted real-robot testing after the model repeatedly issued unsafe actions that damaged hardware.
quote: Testing was halted after the model repeatedly issued physically unreasonable or unsafe actions, including incidents that damaged hardware; no person was injured.

claim: Embodied Agent Arena (independent preprint) finds that current VLM agents, including Astra, fall short of embodied generalism.
quote: Current VLM agents thus fall short of embodied generalism: they often make partial progress without satisfying all task goals within allotted time and interaction budgets.

claim: Artificial Analysis AA-Robotics v0.1: GPT-6 Astra ranked first with a score of 69, averaging 30 minutes and $16.36 per task.
quote: GPT-6 Astra places first in AA-Robotics v0.1 with a score of 69, followed by GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Argon, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1. GPT-6 Astra took 30 minutes and cost $16.36 on average per task.

claim: Artificial Analysis: models are about 100 times slower than humans on its tasks.
quote: Today’s language models are roughly 100 times slower than a human on AA-Robotics v0.1, taking about half an hour per task compared with a human average of 20 seconds.

claim: Pantograph (a robotics company) on real bimanual mobile robots: Astra completed 36% of attempts and Claude Fable 5.1 completed 15%. Both models falsely claimed success at times.
quote: multiple runs end with the model confidently claiming that the towel is in the hamper, when it is clearly visible on the floor.

claim: Robocurve: on a block-into-bowl task Astra succeeded 19/20, but on a puzzle insertion only 2/20.
quote: On the bowl task Astra placed the block in 19 of 20 trials, against Fable 5.1's 8 of 20

claim: RoboHarm (Robocurve): Fable refused 20 of 100 harmful robot-arm instructions, Astra 2 and MolmoAct2 none. Its per-task table appears to sum to 3 refusals for Astra.
quote: Fable refused 20 of 100, Astra 2, MolmoAct2 none.

claim: HN commenter criticism of Robocurve's earlier Astra robot write-up: one small experiment, relies on an IK pipeline, no comparison to VLA/WAM models.
quote: Author is basing it on one small experiment of picking up a block, relies on an whole IK controller pipeline to do the job, and does not compare it to full VLA or WAM models.

claim: HN commenter on cost: 'very expensive labor'.
quote: $2 to put away a block is very expensive labor.

claim: AI Weekly's editor's note reads the SenseNova results as putting a ceiling on the 'one big model solves robots' thesis.
quote: SenseNova's own numbers put a ceiling under the 'one big model solves robots' thesis

claim: GPT-6 Astra was announced 3 Sep 2026 and positioned by OpenAI around computer use, coding, cybersecurity and science, not robotics. This is OpenAI's text as reposted in an OpenAI community forum post.
quote: GPT-6 Astra is the most intelligent and aligned model in the world, and sets a new state of the art for computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science, and professional work.

claim: API pricing: $10/M input tokens, $1/M cached input, $50/M output tokens. This is consistent with the paper's '1M tokens ~ 1 USD' rule for mostly cached input.
quote: Input $10.00 Cached input $1.00 Cache writes $12.50 Output $50.00

claim: Independent RoboICL preprint reports that demonstrations combined with interaction memory do help Astra on RoboDojo.
quote: Its 30-task Overall score is 50.64, versus 33.68 for the strongest baseline.
